analysis.title: Americas Clean Technology: Solar - A quick snapshot of potential implications of 2026 midterm elections
key_insights: GS sees investor focus on midterm implications for solar as muted, citing rising interest rates, overlap with 3Q earnings season, and uncertainty over whether a change in congressional control would produce meaningful policy change.

Based on prediction market expectations, GS sees 2018 as the closest comparison: Democrats won the House against an unsettled policy backdrop. 2026 differs because of a larger solar base and narrower policy incentives.

GS takes no view on the election outcome. It treats the 45X production tax credit as the key sector lever, and expects a House flip to allow enforcement of the existing credit more than to produce new legislation.

After the 2018 midterms, TAN gained about 40% over the next 252 trading days, versus about -20% after 2014 and about -40% after 2022. GS says 2014 and 2022 are poor comparisons because of rapid deployment growth and falling oil prices (2014) and sharply higher rates, supply chain disruption and a post-IRA valuation reset (2022).

In 2018 the sector re-rated once investors gained confidence in the policy boundary, even with Section 201 tariffs still in place. GS infers that clarity on no further policy tightening can support multiple expansion when sentiment is already depressed, as it is now.

The 2018 House flip was followed by legislation introduced in Jul 2019 to extend the 30% solar ITC for five years. The House bill had 29 co-sponsors including four Republicans, versus 16 Senate co-sponsors and no Republicans.

US solar PV capacity rose from about 50GW in 2018 to about 228GW by July 2026 (EIA). A change in control therefore lands on a much larger market where policy visibility affects financing terms, module procurement and interconnection execution.

Under OBBBA, solar facilities that begin construction after July 4, 2026 must be placed in service by December 31, 2027 to qualify for the 45Y or 48E credit. A House flip cannot change this clock but could limit further legislative tightening.

45X gives per-unit production credits for domestically made cells, wafers and battery components. GS says it is central to US solar, battery and inverter manufacturing economics, and that FEOC rules remain an important consideration, with regulations and safe harbor tables still to come.

GS notes that solar's cost advantage makes it unclear whether Congress will extend broad deployment support after OBBBA, but bipartisan support has renewed the 30% ITC several times, so an extension could become more plausible over time.

Democratic leaders have prioritized restoring IRA clean energy credits (Schumer, Jeffries, Wyden), and 122 House Democrats backed the Energy Bills Relief Act in March. Most legislation would still need Senate bipartisan support and could face a Trump veto.

Prediction markets price over 60% odds of a Democratic sweep and under 10% odds of Republicans keeping the House. Democrats led the generic congressional ballot by about 9.0pp as of October 26. GS notes prediction markets have a mixed record and solar sentiment is already weak.

FSLR owns its manufacturing and is fully exposed to the 45X phase-out starting in 2030, so an extension would be a material earnings event. ENPH, SEDG, NXT and ARRY also use 45X but rely on contract manufacturers, which gives them more flexibility to move production.

If Republicans keep the House but lose the Senate, GS sees limited scope to change existing solar tax credits. If Republicans keep both chambers, the existing framework stays the baseline and performance depends on execution.

GS frames the election as a sentiment and policy-risk catalyst, most relevant to the policy path from 2027. It would look for a Democratic gain plus early evidence that control translates into legislation as signals of a stronger sector response.

tension_points.bull_case: A Democratic House reduces the scope for further tightening and could revive discussion of 45X and solar incentives. The 2018 precedent saw TAN gain about 40% over the next 252 trading days and an ITC extension push.
tension_points.bear_case: A House flip alone cannot change the OBBBA construction deadlines. Most legislation needs bipartisan Senate support and President Trump could veto it. Prediction markets have a mixed record and solar sentiment is already weak.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Republicans retaining both chambers, which would leave the existing credit framework as the baseline with no incremental policy upside.
